explanations.explanation: Gold it is, baker. Daniel 3:1 says King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue. Picture a whole statue of shiny gold standing out on that plain, and I'm over here getting excited about a gold base.
Silver is a fine metal, but it isn't what the text says. Daniel 3:1 says the king made a golden statue. Gold is the word the verse uses.
Bronze is a good guess for a big statue, friend. But Daniel 3:1 says King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue. This one was gold, not bronze.
Sixty cubits high, baker. Daniel 3:1 says it was sixty cubits high and six cubits wide. That is a tall, skinny statue, and nobody is getting a hat on that thing.
Twelve is a lot smaller than what the text says, friend. Daniel 3:1 says sixty cubits high and six cubits wide. Sixty is five times what you picked.
Thirty is big, but this statue is double that. Daniel 3:1 says it was sixty cubits high and six cubits wide. Sixty is the number to hold on to.

That's it, baker. Daniel 3:2 says the king sent word to gather all those officials to attend the dedication of the statue he had set up. Think of it as a ribbon cutting, except the statue is the guest of honor.

explanations.answer: To pay the king's new taxes
explanations.explanation: Taxes would make for a grumpy crowd, friend, but the text never mentions them. Daniel 3:2 says the officials were gathered to attend the dedication of the statue. They came for the statue, not for the bills.
Good thinking, since governors are on the guest list. But Daniel 3:2 says the reason was to attend the dedication of the statue. The text never says anything about choosing a new governor.

explanations.answer: Fall down and worship the statue
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Daniel 3:5 says that when they hear the music, they "…must fall down and worship the golden statue…" the king set up. The music was the cue, and the cue was a full band. The list runs from the horn and flute all the way to the pipes and all kinds of music.

explanations.answer: Stand up and sing to the king
explanations.explanation: Singing sounds like a lot more fun, friend, but it's not what the herald said. In Daniel 3:5 the command is to "…fall down and worship the golden statue…" It was down on the ground, not up on your feet.

explanations.answer: Turn around and face the palace
explanations.explanation: Turning around would be an easy one, wouldn't it? The herald asked for more than that. Daniel 3:5 says they must "…fall down and worship the golden statue…" and the statue was the one being worshiped.

Furnace, baker. Daniel 3:6 says whoever does not fall down and worship will immediately be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace. The herald proclaimed it loudly, too. I know a thing or two about hot ovens, and I would not want to stand near that one.

The lions' den is a famous spot in the book of Daniel (Daniel 6:16), so I see why you went there. But that's a different story, and this herald never mentions it. Daniel 3:6 says anyone who doesn't worship will be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace.

A pit is a scary thought, friend, but it isn't what the herald said. Daniel 3:6 says the punishment is being thrown into the blazing fiery furnace. And he says immediately, so there's no waiting around.

True, baker. Daniel 3:7 says that as soon as they heard the music, the people of every nation and language would fall down and worship the golden statue. Everyone went down on cue, every nation and every language. I bet that was something to see, a whole crowd going down at once.

It's true, friend. Daniel 3:7 says that when all the people heard the music, the people of every nation and language would fall down and worship the golden statue. The text shows a whole crowd going down together.
The king himself, baker. In Daniel 3:12 the astrologers say these are Jews the king appointed to manage the province of Babylon. They basically told on someone he had hired.

Arioch is a name from the book of Daniel (Daniel 2:14), but he isn't in this story. Daniel 3:12 has the astrologers telling the king that these are Jews you have appointed. The one who put them in charge was Nebuchadnezzar.

The herald proclaimed the command, friend, but the astrologers point somewhere else. In Daniel 3:12 they tell the king, "…you have appointed…" these men to manage the province. So the appointing came from King Nebuchadnezzar.

Not quite, baker. He was furious, but the king did not throw them in on the spot. Daniel 3:14 says he first asked them, "…is it true that you do not serve my gods or worship the golden statue I have set up?"
False is right, baker. Even furious, the king spoke to them first. In Daniel 3:14 he asks if it is true that they do not serve his gods or worship the statue. Then comes more talking, in verse 15.

explanations.answer: Another chance to bow when the music plays
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Daniel 3:15 says that when they hear the music, if they are ready to fall down and worship the statue, "very good." He gave them a second try, and then he warned them about the furnace.

explanations.answer: A night in prison to think it over
explanations.explanation: A night to think it over would have been a long one, friend, but the text never gives them one. In Daniel 3:15 the king offers another chance to bow when the music plays, right there. The warning follows right behind it.

explanations.answer: A gift of gold if they bow down
explanations.explanation: Gold fits the statue, but the king never offers it as a reward. Daniel 3:15 says he gives them another chance to fall down when the music plays. If they refuse, they will be thrown at once into the furnace.

explanations.answer: Deliver them from the furnace and the king's hand
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. In Daniel 3:17 they say, "If the God whom we serve exists, then He is able to deliver us from the blazing fiery furnace and from your hand, O king." They name both the furnace and the king, and they say it right to his face.

explanations.answer: Make the king forget about his decree
explanations.explanation: That would make for a quiet afternoon, wouldn't it? But it isn't what they say. Daniel 3:17 says God is able to deliver them "…from the blazing fiery furnace and from your hand, O king."

explanations.answer: Crush the golden statue into dust
explanations.explanation: A statue crushed to dust would be quite a show, friend, but they never ask for it. In Daniel 3:17 they say God is able to deliver them from the furnace and from the king's hand. Their words are about them being delivered.

Not at all, baker. Their answer is the opposite. Daniel 3:18 says, "But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up."

False, and what a line it is, baker. Daniel 3:18 says, "But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up." They stay put whichever way it goes.

Seven, baker. Daniel 3:19 says he gave orders to heat the furnace seven times hotter than usual. It was Nebuchadnezzar who gave that order. I burn a batch at the regular heat and I'm still sorry about it for days.
Three is a nice number, since there are three men, but it's not the one. Daniel 3:19 says he gave orders to heat the furnace seven times hotter than usual. It's seven, friend.
Ten is a lovely round number, but the text doesn't use it. Daniel 3:19 says he ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. Seven is what the king wanted.

Yes, baker, and it's a heavy part. Daniel 3:22 says the king's command was so urgent and the furnace so hot that the flames killed the men who carried the three up. That tells us how hot it really was.

The text doesn't say they ran, friend. Daniel 3:22 says the king's command was so urgent and the furnace so hot that the flames killed the men who carried Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego up. It's a heavy detail, and it shows how hot that furnace was.
The text doesn't say they refused, friend. Daniel 3:22 says the king's command was so urgent and the furnace so hot that the flames killed the men who carried the three up. It's a heavy moment.
Four, baker, not three. In Daniel 3:25 the king says, "I see four men, unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire…" They went in firmly bound and now nothing is tying anybody up.

explanations.answer: Three men lying still in the flames
explanations.explanation: That's not what the king saw, friend. Daniel 3:25 says, "I see four men, unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire…" Walking around, and four instead of three.

explanations.answer: The fire dying down to ashes
explanations.explanation: The fire was still going, friend. The king looked in and was amazed. In Daniel 3:25 he says, "I see four men, unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire…"

explanations.answer: Servants of the Most High God
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. In Daniel 3:26 the king calls out, "Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out!" Quite a change from the guy who was furious with rage a few verses back.

explanations.answer: Traitors to the king of Babylon
explanations.explanation: That's what you'd expect after all that rage, friend. But at the furnace door the king speaks differently. In Daniel 3:26 he calls them "…servants of the Most High God…"
Nice compliment, but it isn't what he says. In Daniel 3:26 the king calls to them, "…servants of the Most High God, come out!" He names their God, not their wisdom.
Nope, baker, it's the other way around. Daniel 3:27 says there was no smell of fire on them. Not a hair of their heads was singed, and their robes were unaffected.

False, baker. Daniel 3:27 says the fire had no effect on their bodies, and there was no smell of fire on them. Not a hair of their heads was singed, either. They came out of a furnace seven times hotter than usual and didn't smell like it.

His angel, baker. In Daniel 3:28 Nebuchadnezzar says, "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent His angel and delivered His servants who trusted in Him." Those are the king's own words.
A prophet is a reasonable guess, friend. But Daniel 3:28 has the king say that God "…has sent His angel…" Angel is the word he uses.
A priest isn't who the king names, friend. In Daniel 3:28 the king says God "…has sent His angel and delivered His servants…" It's an angel in his words.

True, baker. In Daniel 3:29 the king decrees that anyone of any nation or language who says anything offensive against the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego will be cut into pieces. The decree also says their houses would be reduced to rubble. It's a harsh decree, and it's what the text says.

It's true, friend, even though it's a rough one to read. Daniel 3:29 says the king decrees that anyone who says anything offensive against their God will be cut into pieces, and their houses reduced to rubble. It's a heavy line, but that's the text.

Promoted, baker. Daniel 3:30 says the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the province of Babylon. It's the same province they were already managing. They went from the furnace to a better job.
After all that, banishing them would have been a sad ending, friend. But it isn't what happened. Daniel 3:30 says the king promoted them in the province of Babylon.
Prison is a long way from where this story lands, friend. Daniel 3:30 says the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the province of Babylon. They walked out of the fire and kept going up.
